title: BFS Level Order
description: BFS with a queue, processing one level per outer iteration by snapshotting the queue size before the inner loop.

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the inputs.
sections.say:
"So I need to return the level-order traversal of a binary tree as an array of arrays — one inner array per level, containing the values at that depth in left-to-right order. For tree [3,9,20,null,null,15,7], the answer is [[3],[9,20],[15,7]]. Yes?"

Then a few quick clarifying questions:
• Empty tree — return `[]` or `[[]]`? (I'd argue `[]` — no levels, not one empty level.)
• Are levels guaranteed to be in left-to-right order? (Yes is standard.)
• Node shape — `{ val, left, right }` with `null` children?
• Could the tree have a single skewed branch? (Affects max queue width but not the algorithm.)
sections.why: The `[]` vs `[[]]` distinction on empty input is a real bug magnet — both are plausible interpretations and the wrong choice fails a single test case at the bottom of the suite. Asking up front beats discovering it post-hoc. The left-to-right ordering question matters because BFS naturally produces it only if you enqueue left before right; flipping that order would produce right-to-left, which is a different problem.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the obvious — DFS with depth — before pivoting to BFS.
sections.say:
"One option is recursive DFS carrying a `depth` parameter: at each node, push its value into `res[depth]`, recursing left and right with `depth + 1`. That's O(n) time and gives the right answer because depth-first naturally fills levels in left-to-right order if you recurse left first.

The BFS version is the more idiomatic answer for level-order — it processes one level at a time in lockstep with the structure of the question, and the level boundaries fall out naturally from the queue size. I'd go with BFS because the code reads as 'for each level, collect its values, then enqueue the next level' — that's literally what the problem asks for."
sections.why: Two reasons to mention the DFS variant out loud. (1) It proves you can see both approaches and chose BFS deliberately, not because you didn't think of DFS. (2) It frames BFS as 'the more natural fit for level-order' rather than 'the only way' — which is what an interviewer wants to hear. They're grading on judgment about which tool fits, not memorization of one canonical answer.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.prompt: What signal in the problem points to BFS with a level-size snapshot?
sections.say:
"Level-order with explicit per-level grouping is the canonical 'BFS with level-size trick' problem. The standard BFS template visits nodes one at a time, but here I need to know which level each node belongs to — and the trick for that is to snapshot `queue.length` BEFORE the inner loop, then process exactly that many nodes. Any children pushed during the inner loop belong to the NEXT level, not the current one, so the snapshot captures the level boundary precisely.

This is THE template for any 'do something per level' problem: right-side view, average per level, max per level, zigzag traversal — they all share this skeleton."
sections.why: Naming the level-size snapshot trick — and explaining WHY it works (children pushed mid-loop go to the next level) — is the move. 'BFS' alone is the right pattern name but not the right depth; specifying the snapshot mechanism shows you understand the implementation pitfall that catches most people. The 'this is THE template' callout demonstrates you see the reusable shape across the BFS family, not just this question.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few inputs to confirm the model before writing the loop.
sections.intro: "Let me trace through a couple of cases to make sure my model is right." Three inputs cover the interesting behaviors — the classic mixed-sparse tree, the empty tree, and a perfectly balanced one.

examples.note: Classic — sparse mid-level (9 has no children, 20 has two).
examples.trace:
queue=[3], res=[]
iter 1: size=1, level=[]
  shift 3 → level=[3], enqueue 9, 20. queue=[9,20]
  level done → res=[[3]]
iter 2: size=2, level=[]
  shift 9 → level=[9], no children. queue=[20]
  shift 20 → level=[9,20], enqueue 15, 7. queue=[15,7]
  level done → res=[[3],[9,20]]
iter 3: size=2, level=[]
  shift 15 → level=[15], no children. queue=[7]
  shift 7 → level=[15,7], no children. queue=[]
  level done → res=[[3],[9,20],[15,7]]
queue empty → return [[3],[9,20],[15,7]]

examples.note: Perfectly balanced — level widths double each iteration.
examples.trace:
queue=[1], res=[]
iter 1: size=1 → shift 1, enqueue 2,3. res=[[1]]. queue=[2,3]
iter 2: size=2 → shift 2 (enqueue 4,5), shift 3 (enqueue 6,7). res=[[1],[2,3]]. queue=[4,5,6,7]
iter 3: size=4 → shift 4,5,6,7 (no children). res=[[1],[2,3],[4,5,6,7]]. queue=[]
return [[1],[2,3],[4,5,6,7]]

sections.why: The mixed-sparse trace surfaces the level-snapshot bug — if you accidentally used `queue.length` INSIDE the inner loop instead of the snapshotted `size`, iter 2 would see queue grow to 4 mid-loop and process 15 and 7 as part of level 2. Watching the snapshot stay fixed while the queue grows is the visual proof the trick works. The empty case defends the early return; without it you'd return `[[]]` instead of `[]`.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Before I declare it done, let me think about edges:
• Null root → returns `[]` via early guard. (Without the guard you'd return `[[]]` because the outer while wouldn't execute but an empty level would be pushed by... wait, no, without the guard the while loop wouldn't run at all because `queue.length` is 0 — you'd actually return `[]` correctly. The guard is still cleaner.) ✓
• Single node → returns `[[v]]`. ✓
• Left-skewed (degenerate to linked list) → each level has exactly one node, res has n inner arrays of length 1.
• Right-skewed → same as left-skewed, mirror image.
• Perfectly balanced → max queue width is n/2 at the bottom level, so O(n) extra space worst case.
• Very wide tree (e.g. a root with 1000 children — wait, this is binary, so at most 2 — but a perfectly balanced tree with 1M leaves would have 500K nodes in the queue simultaneously). For huge trees, that O(w) memory matters.
• Performance: `queue.shift()` is O(n) in JS arrays — for large trees, total cost becomes O(n²). The fix is a head index (`let head = 0; const node = queue[head++]`) or a real deque."
sections.why: The `shift` O(n) callout is the senior signal. Most candidates write `queue.shift()` and move on; flagging that it's O(n) and offering the head-index fix shows you know the JS performance gotcha that doesn't bite on LeetCode test cases but bites hard in production. Interviewers love this because it's specifically about JavaScript, not about the algorithm — it proves you know the language, not just the textbook.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time is O(n) — each node is enqueued exactly once and dequeued exactly once. The level-size snapshot adds zero overhead per node; the per-level inner loop just slices the work into chunks.

With the naive `queue.shift()` it's actually O(n²) on huge inputs because `shift` walks the whole array each call. For interview purposes O(n) is the right answer to state, but I'd flag the gotcha and offer the head-index fix if the interviewer probes.

Space is O(w) where w is the maximum level width — at most n/2 for a balanced tree at the bottom level, so O(n) worst case.

If you wanted to extend to right-side view (LeetCode 199), it's the same skeleton — just push only the LAST element of each level instead of all of them. For zigzag traversal (LeetCode 103), alternate `level.push` and `level.unshift` (or reverse the level after building). Same template, different per-level processing."
sections.why: The `shift` amortization caveat is what wins the pushback — interviewers who care about performance will ask, and pre-empting it shows you do too. The right-side-view and zigzag extensions prove you see this as a reusable template, not just this problem's solution. That's the difference between memorizing one answer and understanding a pattern family.

walkthrough.intro: Step through level-order BFS one statement at a time. Watch the queue evolve as each level is snapshotted and drained.
trace: if (!arr || arr.length === 0 || arr[0] == null) return null;
const root = { val: arr[0], left: null, right: null };
if (i < arr.length && arr[i] != null) { node.left = { val: arr[i], left: null, right: null }; q.push(node.left); }
if (i < arr.length && arr[i] != null) { node.right = { val: arr[i], left: null, right: null }; q.push(node.right); }
yield { line: 1, label: `enter levelOrder — tree ${JSON.stringify(input)}`, state: { treeShape: input } };
yield { line: 2, label: 'root is null → return []', state: { treeShape: input, returns: JSON.stringify([]) } };
yield { line: 3, label: 'init res=[]', state: { treeShape: input, res } };
yield { line: 4, label: `init queue=[${root.val}]`, state: { treeShape: input, res, queue: queue.map(n => n.val) } };
yield { line: 6, label: `outer iter — snapshot size=${size} (this level only)`, state: { treeShape: input, res, queue: queue.map(n => n.val), size } };
yield { line: 7, label: 'init level=[]', state: { treeShape: input, res, queue: queue.map(n => n.val), size, level } };
yield { line: 9, label: `shift node ${node.val}`, state: { treeShape: input, res, queue: queue.map(n => n.val), size, i, level: [...level], node: node.val } };
yield { line: 10, label: `push ${node.val} into level → [${level.join(',')}]`, state: { treeShape: input, res, queue: queue.map(n => n.val), size, i, level: [...level] } };
if (node.left)  { queue.push(node.left);  yield { line: 11, label: `enqueue left  ${node.left.val}`,  state: { treeShape: input, res, queue: queue.map(n => n.val), size, i, level: [...level] } }; }
if (node.right) { queue.push(node.right); yield { line: 12, label: `enqueue right ${node.right.val}`, state: { treeShape: input, res, queue: queue.map(n => n.val), size, i, level: [...level] } }; }
yield { line: 14, label: `level done — push [${level.join(',')}] into res`, state: { treeShape: input, res: res.map(l => [...l]), queue: queue.map(n => n.val) } };

reference.approach: BFS queue with a per-level size snapshot
notes: Snapshot queue.length BEFORE the inner loop — children pushed during the loop belong to the NEXT level.
Guard the root: if root is null return [] (not [[]]).
Array.shift is O(n); for very large trees prefer a head index or a real deque.

alternates.label: DFS with depth parameter
alternates.when: Use when you're already doing DFS for a related computation and want to avoid a second pass, or when the interviewer asks for a recursive solution. Same O(n) time; uses O(h) stack space instead of O(w) queue space — better for deep-but-narrow trees.
notes: When `depth === res.length` the bucket for this level doesn't exist yet — create it before pushing.
Pre-order (self before children) ensures the left child is always appended before the right within each level bucket.
Space is O(h) for the recursion stack — strictly better than BFS on tall-narrow trees; strictly worse on wide trees where h ≈ log n but w ≈ n/2.

questions.q: Why snapshot queue.length into `size` before the inner loop?
options: So `queue.shift()` becomes O(1) once the length is cached in a local
Because children pushed during the loop belong to the next level
So the loop terminates before the queue grows past its initial capacity
To skip the final level whose children would otherwise be re-enqueued
questions.explain: `queue.push(node.left)` grows the queue mid-loop, so reading `queue.length` inside the `for` would let the next level bleed into the current one. The frozen `size` pins the level boundary.

options: O(n) — each node enqueued and dequeued once
questions.explain: Every node is pushed once and shifted once; the level snapshot only chunks that same work. Caveat worth stating out loud: `Array.shift()` is O(n) in JS, so the literal code is O(n²) on huge trees unless you swap in a head index.

questions.q: For a null root, the function returns:
questions.explain: The `if (!root) return []` guard fires. An empty tree has zero levels, so `[[]]` — one level that happens to be empty — is the wrong shape.

questions.q: Which data structure is BFS built on?
questions.explain: FIFO is what keeps siblings adjacent and defers children until the current level drains. Swap in a LIFO stack and the same loop dives down one branch first — that's DFS.

questions.q: If you swapped the queue for a stack (LIFO) — pop from the back instead of shift from the front — what traversal would you get?
options: Depth-first (DFS) — a stack dives down one branch before backtracking, not level by level
questions.explain: FIFO queue → BFS (breadth, level by level); LIFO stack → DFS (depth-first). The data structure IS the difference between the two.

questions.q: Core distinction: when do you reach for BFS over DFS on a tree?
options: BFS for balanced trees, DFS for skewed trees — the queue width determines which is feasible
BFS when you need shortest-path/level info or to process nodes nearest-first; DFS when you explore each branch fully (subtree aggregates, path-to-leaf problems)
BFS guarantees O(log n) for any tree question because it processes levels; DFS is O(n)
DFS for any problem that returns a single value, BFS for any problem that returns an array
questions.explain: BFS expands by distance from the root (great for levels and shortest unweighted paths); DFS goes deep first (great for subtree/path computations).

options: O(h) where h is the height
O(w) where w is the max level width — the queue can hold a whole level at once
questions.explain: The queue holds at most one level; the widest level of a balanced tree is ~n/2, so worst case is O(n). DFS, by contrast, is O(h).

questions.q: To get 'right-side view' (the last node visible at each level), what is the minimal change to this template?
options: Switch the queue to a stack
Inside the level loop, only record the node when `i === size - 1` (the last one in the level)
questions.explain: Right-side view is the same level snapshot; you just keep the last node of each level instead of all of them.

questions.q: For zig-zag (boustrophedon) level order, how do you adapt the template?
options: Use a stack instead of a queue
Build each level normally, but reverse (or unshift into) every other level before pushing it to the result
questions.explain: The BFS structure is unchanged; you just flip the direction of every other level when emitting it.
